title: Stacks, expressions and recursion
subtitle: Last in, first out — and why that is exactly the shape of function calls. The chapter builds the stack, uses it to evaluate and convert expressions, then shows recursion as the stack in disguise, ending with the classic recursive algorithms.

stack.title: The stack ADT
stack.body:
Think of a stack of plates in a canteen. You add a plate on top and take a plate from the top; to reach the plate at the bottom you must remove everything above it. A stack behaves exactly like this: insertion and removal happen at one end only, the top. The operations are push (add on top), pop (remove and return the top), peek or top (read the top without removing) and isEmpty. The last item pushed is the first popped — LIFO, last in, first out.

As an ADT, a stack is only this contract. Two implementations are common. In an array, an integer top records the index of the top element (−1 when empty); push increments it and stores, pop returns and decrements. The size is fixed, so pushing onto a full stack is overflow and must be checked, as must underflow (popping an empty stack). In a linked list, push inserts a new node at the head and pop removes the head — no size limit apart from memory. Both give O(1) for every operation, which is the stack’s selling point. C++ provides std::stack built on a deque; the program below pushes 10, 20, 30, 40 and pops them back in reverse order.

apps.title: What stacks are used for
apps.body:
Whenever something must be undone in reverse order, a stack appears. The undo command in an editor pushes each action and pops it to reverse. A web browser’s back button is a stack of visited pages. The run-time system uses a stack for function calls — each call pushes a frame holding its parameters, local variables and return address, and each return pops it — which is the subject of the recursion sections below. Compilers use stacks to check balanced brackets, to convert and evaluate expressions, and to parse nested constructs. Algorithms use them to simulate recursion (depth-first search) and for backtracking (maze solving).

The bracket-matching algorithm is the cleanest first example. Scan the text left to right; on an opening bracket (, [ or { push it; on a closing bracket, the stack must be non-empty and its top must be the matching opening bracket — pop it; any mismatch is an error; at the end the stack must be empty. Run it on {[()]}(: the first six characters match perfectly, but the final “(” is never closed, so the stack is not empty and the text is not balanced.

postfix.title: Expressions: infix, prefix and postfix
postfix.body:
We normally write arithmetic in infix notation, with the operator between its operands: A + B. It is ambiguous without rules — what does A + B × C mean? — so we need precedence (× before +), associativity (left to right for − and /; right to left for exponentiation) and parentheses to override them. In postfix (reverse Polish, Łukasiewicz in reverse) the operator follows its operands: A B +. In prefix (Polish) it precedes them: + A B. Both are unambiguous without parentheses or precedence, because the position of each operator already says what it applies to. That makes them ideal for a machine, and a stack evaluates them effortlessly.

Evaluating postfix is mechanical: scan left to right; push each operand; on an operator, pop the top two values (the first popped is the right operand), apply the operator, push the result. At the end the stack holds the answer. For 2 3 * 5 4 * + 9 −: push 2, 3; × gives 6; push 5, 4; × gives 20; + gives 26… the run below computes 6 + 20 − 9 = 17.

Converting infix to postfix (Dijkstra’s shunting-yard algorithm) uses a stack of operators. Read tokens left to right. An operand goes straight to the output. For an operator, pop and output any stacked operator of higher or equal precedence (for left-associative operators), then push it. “(” is pushed; “)” pops and outputs until the matching “(” (which is discarded). At the end pop everything to the output. A + B × C − (D / E) becomes A B C * + D E / -. Step the card: the stack is the lower row, the output the row above.
postfix.steps: Evaluate the postfix of (2+3)*4−6/2 using a stack of numbers: push operands, each operator pops two. 2 3 + → 5; 5 4 × → 20; 6 2 / → 3; 20 3 − → 17. Order matters for − and /: when popping, the first value is the right operand. For 6 2 / the stack holds [6, 2]; pop gives b = 2 then a = 6, so the result is a / b = 3, not 2 / 6.

rec.title: Recursion: a function that calls itself
rec.body:
Some problems contain smaller copies of themselves. To compute n!, note that n! = n × (n − 1)!: the factorial of n is n times the factorial of something smaller. A recursive function exploits this by calling itself on the smaller problem. Every correct recursive function has two parts: a base case that is answered directly (0! = 1) and stops the recursion, and a recursive case that reduces the problem and calls the function again, moving towards the base case. Leave out the base case, or fail to approach it, and the calls never stop.

How does the machine keep track? Each call gets its own activation record (stack frame) on the call stack, holding its parameters, its local variables and where to return. A new call pushes a frame; a return pops it. The run-time stack is the stack ADT of the previous sections, used by the machine itself. That is why a recursion that goes a million levels deep crashes with a stack overflow: it has run out of frame space. Run the factorial program and watch the stack grow five frames deep, then unwind as each pending multiplication completes.

Trace the figure: fact(4) calls fact(3), which calls fact(2), then fact(1) — the base case, which returns 1 without calling anything. Now the frames pop in reverse order: fact(2) returns 2 × 1 = 2, fact(3) returns 3 × 2 = 6, fact(4) returns 4 × 6 = 24. Nothing is multiplied on the way down; all the work happens on the way back up.

examples.title: Classic recursive algorithms
examples.body:
Four short programs teach most of what exams ask. Greatest common divisor (Euclid): gcd(a, b) = a if b = 0, otherwise gcd(b, a mod b). Each call shrinks the second argument, so it must reach 0. gcd(48, 18) → gcd(18, 12) → gcd(12, 6) → gcd(6, 0) = 6. Digit sum: sumDigits(n) = n if n < 10 else (n mod 10) + sumDigits(n / 10); 9045 gives 5 + 4 + 0 + 9 = 18. Fast exponentiation: x^n = (x^{n/2})² for even n and x·(x^{n/2})² for odd n — halving the exponent gives O(log n) multiplications instead of n; power(2, 10) needs only 5 calls. Binary search (next chapters) is the same halving idea on a sorted array.

Compare fast exponentiation with the obvious loop. Computing 2¹⁰ naively takes 10 multiplications; the recursive halving version takes five calls (n = 10, 5, 2, 1, 0). For exponent a million that is 1,000,000 against about 20: the difference between a design that works and one that does not.
examples.steps: Trace gcd(48, 18). Continue until the second argument is 0. The base case returns a.

hanoi.title: Tower of Hanoi
hanoi.body:
Three pegs, A, B and C. Peg A holds n disks of decreasing size, the largest at the bottom. Move them all to C, one at a time, never placing a larger disk on a smaller one, using B as a spare. Try it by hand with n = 4 and you will be lost; think recursively and it is trivial. To move n disks from A to C: first move the top n − 1 disks from A to B (using C as the spare), then move the largest disk from A to C, then move the n − 1 disks from B to C (using A). The two sub-moves are the same problem with one disk fewer. The base case is zero disks: do nothing.

Counting the moves gives a recurrence. Let T(n) be the number of moves. Then T(n) = T(n − 1) + 1 + T(n − 1) = 2T(n − 1) + 1 with T(0) = 0. Unrolling shows T(n) = 2ⁿ − 1: T(1) = 1, T(2) = 3, T(3) = 7, T(4) = 15. The cost is exponential — adding a single disk doubles the work — and it is provably the minimum number of moves, so no cleverness avoids it. The legend says monks move 64 golden disks; at one move a second that is 2⁶⁴ − 1 seconds, about 585 billion years.
hanoi.steps: The recursion makes two calls on n − 1 disks and one direct move. Unroll once and twice to see the pattern. After k steps the coefficient of T is 2^k and the constant is 2^k − 1. Stop at k = n where T(0) = 0. T(1) = 1 and T(n) = 2T(n−1) + 1. Expanding: T(n) = 2ⁿ − 1.

types.title: Kinds of recursion and the cost of recursion
types.body:
Recursion comes in several shapes. In direct recursion a function calls itself; in indirect (mutual) recursion f calls g and g calls f. In linear recursion each call makes at most one further call (factorial, gcd); in binary or tree recursion each makes two (Fibonacci, Hanoi), which is where exponential costs hide. A call is tail recursive if the recursive call is the very last thing the function does — there is nothing left to do after it returns, such as the multiplication in n * fact(n-1). A tail-recursive function can be turned into a loop automatically (tail-call optimisation) so it uses no extra stack; the factorial above is not tail recursive, but the accumulator version fact(n, acc) = fact(n − 1, n·acc) is.

The costs of recursion are time (call overhead) and space (a frame per pending call, O(depth)). The danger is repeated work. The naive Fibonacci function recomputes the same values over and over: fib(10) makes 177 calls for an answer that needs only 10 additions. Remember the answers in a table — memoisation — and each value is computed once; fib(10) then makes only 19 calls. This is the seed of dynamic programming: when subproblems overlap, recursion needs a memory.

iter.title: Recursion versus iteration and backtracking
iter.body:
Anything recursive can be written with a loop and an explicit stack, because the call stack is a stack; and any loop can be written as tail recursion. Which to use? Recursion is natural when the problem or the data is recursive — trees, divide-and-conquer, backtracking — and the code mirrors the definition. Iteration is usually faster and uses O(1) stack, and is safer for very deep problems. A good rule: use recursion when it makes the algorithm clearer and the depth is modest (log n or at most a few thousand); use a loop when the recursion is linear and the depth could be large.

Backtracking is recursion with an undo step. To solve a puzzle (eight queens, a maze, sudoku) you make a choice, recurse to try to complete the solution, and if you reach a dead end you undo the choice and try the next. The recursion stack remembers where to back up to. The same idea explains depth-first search in graphs, which we use two chapters from now.

summary.title: Summary
summary.body:
• A stack is LIFO with O(1) push, pop and peek; check overflow and underflow. It powers undo, back, bracket matching, expression handling and the call stack.
  • Postfix needs no parentheses: evaluate with a stack of numbers; convert from infix with a stack of operators (shunting-yard).
  • Recursion = base case + a smaller problem; each active call has a stack frame; work happens as frames return.
  • Classics: factorial, gcd (Euclid), digit sum, fast exponentiation (log n), Hanoi (2ⁿ − 1 moves).
  • Tree recursion can be exponential (naive Fibonacci); memoisation fixes it. Tail recursion can become a loop. Backtracking is recursion with undo.
